\chapter{Going, and the Future You Can Already Say}
\label{ch:ir-y-futuro}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask where someone is going, say what a singular person is going to do, and mark a known singular noun with mi, tu, or su.}

Complete ES-C10-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise with singular ir, ir a plus a known infinitive, and mi, tu, or su before café.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ir]{ir — “to go,” from more than one historical stem}

\label{lesson:ES-C10-ir}



\begin{quote}
You already match different verb forms with \textbf{tú} and \textbf{usted}, and you can ask \textbf{¿Dónde…?}, “Where…?” Today, add one new verb and only its three singular-person forms.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-i} — \textbf{ir} is one clear syllable, like \emph{ear} without a glide.
  \item \texttt{diphthong-oy} — \textbf{voy} ends with the sound in English \emph{boy}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ir} means “to go.” Its infinitive descends from Latin \textbf{īre}, also “to go.” The present forms below followed a different Latin verb, \textbf{vādere}, “to go forward” or “advance.” English \textbf{invade} and \textbf{evade} preserve that \emph{vad-} family.

One modern verb built from historically different stems is called \textbf{suppletive}. English does the same thing when \emph{go} changes to \emph{went}, an old form borrowed from \emph{wend}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: only three forms today}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{ir}} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{voy} \\
tú & \textbf{vas} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{va} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say the small set as \textbf{voy · vas · va}. The plural forms are deliberately left for a later lesson.

The known question word now gives you a useful prompt:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{¿Dónde va usted?} — “Where are you going?”
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “ir — voy, vas, va”
  \item “¿Dónde va usted?”
  \item “īre gives ir; vādere gives the present set”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ir} mean? (“To go.”) Give the three forms learned today. (\emph{Voy, vas, va.}) Why do they look unlike \emph{ir}? (The infinitive and present set come through different Latin stems.) Next: place \textbf{a} and a known infinitive after this small set to talk about what is coming.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[voy a + infinitive]{voy a + infinitive — moving toward the near future}

\label{lesson:ES-C10-ir-a-futuro}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{voy, vas, va} and the infinitives \textbf{hablar, comer, vivir}. This lesson joins those owned pieces with one short new word.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish \textbf{a} means “to” or “toward.” It descends from Latin \textbf{ad}, “toward,” which English keeps in words such as \textbf{advance}.

Movement toward a place easily becomes movement toward a future event. English uses the same picture in “I am \textbf{going to} speak.” Spanish keeps \textbf{a} visible: \textbf{voy a hablar}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: ir + a + an unchanged infinitive}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{near-future frame} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{voy a hablar} & I am going to speak \\
tú & \textbf{vas a comer} & you are going to eat \\
usted & \textbf{va a vivir} & you are going to live \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Only \textbf{ir} changes for the person. The second verb stays in its known dictionary form: \textbf{hablar}, \textbf{comer}, or \textbf{vivir}. No new plural person or infinitive is hidden in the pattern.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “voy a hablar”
  \item “vas a comer”
  \item “va a vivir”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the frame? (\emph{Ir} in the present + \textbf{a} + an infinitive.) Does the second verb change for the person? (No.) What idea connects physical going with future time? (Motion toward a destination becomes motion toward an event.) Next: say whose already-known \textbf{café} it is.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hablaré]{hablaré — the future in one word}

\label{lesson:ES-C10-futuro-simple}



\begin{quote}
You can already say \emph{voy a hablar} — \textquotedblleft{}I am going to speak.\textquotedblright{} Spanish has a second way to say the same thing, and it is shorter: one word instead of three. Your job here is to recognize it and to see where it came from.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item voy a + infinitive — the future you already have.
  \item hablar — the infinitive this is built on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-e} — the ending is stressed: \emph{hablarÉ} (\emph{ah-blah-REH}). The written accent is doing real work; it tells you where your voice lifts. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hablaré} — \textquotedblleft{}I will speak.\textquotedblright{} Look closely and you will see a word you already know sitting inside it, whole and unchanged:

\texttt{}\texttt{ hablar   +   é      $\to$   hablaré (to speak)   (ending)     (I will speak) }\texttt{}

This is the one Spanish tense built on the \textbf{complete infinitive}. Nothing is chopped off. Every other tense you have met removes the \emph{-ar} first; this one leaves it alone and simply adds to the end.

\textbf{Where the ending comes from.} It is a verb in its own right, worn down. Latin speakers said \emph{hablare habeo} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I have} to speak,\textquotedblright{} in the sense of \textquotedblleft{}I am to speak,\textquotedblright{} a thing still ahead of me. Said often enough, the \emph{habeo} shrank onto the back of the infinitive and stopped being a separate word:

\texttt{}\texttt{ hablare habeo   $\to$   hablar é   $\to$   hablaré "I have to speak"                  "I will speak" }\texttt{}

So the Spanish future is an obligation that turned into a prediction — the same drift English made when \textquotedblleft{}I \textbf{shall} speak\textquotedblright{} softened out of a word that once meant \textquotedblleft{}I owe.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The singular endings ride on the full infinitive, and they are the \textbf{same for all three verb families} — \emph{-ar}, \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} alike. This is the most regular tense in the language:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{speak} & \textbf{eat} & \textbf{live} \\
\midrule
I will & hablaré & comeré & viviré \\
you will & hablarás & comerás & vivirás \\
he/she will & hablará & comerá & vivirá \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both futures are correct. \emph{Voy a hablar} is what you will hear most in conversation; \emph{hablaré} is a little more formal, and is what you will meet in writing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hablaré} — stress the last syllable
  \item the same idea the long way — \emph{voy a hablar}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I will eat\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I will live,\textquotedblright{} using the table
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What whole word can you still see inside \emph{hablaré}? (\emph{hablar}.) Which syllable carries the stress? (The last — the accent says so.) The ending began life as which Latin verb? (\emph{Habeo}, \textquotedblleft{}I have.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mi, tu, su]{mi, tu, su — whose café?}

\label{lesson:ES-C10-mi-tu-su}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{café}, and you distinguish informal \textbf{tú} from formal \textbf{usted}. Now put one small ownership word before that one known noun.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{Latin source} & \textbf{meaning in today's frame} \\
\midrule
\textbf{mi} & \emph{meus} & my \\
\textbf{tu} & \emph{tuus} & your, to one informal \textbf{tú} \\
\textbf{su} & \emph{suus} & your, to formal \textbf{usted}; also his or her \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English \textbf{my} helps recall \textbf{mi}. Older English \textbf{thy}, “your,” helps recall Latin \emph{tuus} and Spanish \textbf{tu}. The ownership word \textbf{tu} has no written accent; the person word \textbf{tú} that you already know keeps its accent.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: put the ownership word before the noun}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{phrase} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\textbf{mi café} & my coffee \\
\textbf{tu café} & your coffee, informal \\
\textbf{su café} & your coffee, formal; or his or her coffee \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The situation tells you which person \textbf{su} points to. Every noun phrase in this lesson is singular. Forms used before plural things are left for a later step, so there is no new number pattern to learn here.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “mi café”
  \item “tu café” to \emph{tú}
  \item “su café” to \emph{usted}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three ownership words. (\emph{Mi, tu, su.}) Where do they go? (Before the noun.) Which one addresses \emph{usted}? (\emph{Su.}) Which Latin sources sit behind them? (\emph{Meus, tuus, suus.}) Next: retrieve the chapter without adding a new word, form, or noun.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — going, approaching events, and ownership}

\label{lesson:ES-C10-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve \textbf{voy, vas, va}; build the near future with \textbf{a} and a known infinitive; then put \textbf{mi, tu,} or \textbf{su} before the known noun \textbf{café}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the complete small chapter frame}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ir}, singular: \textbf{voy · vas · va}.
  \item near future: \textbf{voy a hablar · vas a comer · va a vivir}.
  \item ownership before one singular known noun: \textbf{mi café · tu café · su café}.
\end{itemize}

Plural person forms of \emph{ir} and possessives before plural nouns remain deferred.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ir} continues Latin \emph{īre}, while \textbf{voy, vas, va} continue \emph{vādere}.
  \item \textbf{a} continues Latin \emph{ad}, “toward”; motion toward a goal became motion toward a coming event.
  \item \textbf{mi, tu, su} continue Latin \emph{meus, tuus, suus}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “voy, vas, va”
  \item “voy a hablar, vas a comer, va a vivir”
  \item “mi café, tu café, su café”
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} “Voy a hablar. Su café.”

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the singular \emph{ir} set. (\emph{Voy, vas, va.}) Build “You are going to eat” for one friend. (\emph{Vas a comer.}) Say “my coffee” and formal “your coffee.” (\emph{Mi café; su café.}) The next chapter can now extend the grammar from this small, closed frontier.
\end{tcolorbox}
